title: Parse vs Tokenize: CPU bottleneck hypotheses and synthetic benchmark plan
content:
Summary:

Working doc to prioritize and run a set of focused synthetic benchmarks and lightweight production samplers to answer: for small-to-medium requests, is the dominant CPU work request serialization/deserialization (JSON/header) or tokenization/encoding (BPE/unicode scanning), and how much of the remainder is Python object allocation / thread scheduling overhead?

Context / motivation:
- We observe persistent elevated CPU tail (p95/p99) on smaller requests despite GPU tokens being small; flamegraphs from previous runs suggest a wide tail of ~15-40ms in the pre-inference path. Existing notes touched GIL and tokenizer hotspots, but there is ambiguity about where to invest: faster JSON parsing, C-accelerated tokenizers, or redesigned worker handoff.
- This plan aims to measure relative contributions reproducibly and propose mitigations with measurable impact on per-request CPU cost and tail latency.

High-level hypotheses (ranked):
1) For very small payloads (<= 150 bytes prompt), JSON deserialization + header parsing + validation is >=50% of CPU pre-inference cost. Using a C parser (simdjson) or avoiding full deserialization (manual header parse) will materially reduce CPU time.
2) For typical chat-like payloads (500-1500 bytes), tokenization (unicode scanning, BPE matching) dominates CPU but benefits greatly from a C tokenizer and pre-tokenization caching.
3) Python-level allocations (creating dicts/strings, copying slices) + cooperative thread pool handoff create a non-trivial scheduling tail (5-20ms) even when native code does most work. Subinterpreters or reducing copies reduces tail.
4) Combining (1) and (3) creates a multiplicative tail: fast parser + slow Python dance still leaves residual latency; need both sides addressed for best p99 improvement.

Success metrics / acceptance criteria:
- For tiny payloads (<=150B): end-to-end pre-inference CPU wall time reduced by >=40% on synthetic runs and >=25% in sampled production traffic.
- For mid payloads (500B-1.5KB): tokenization CPU reduced by >=35% and p95/p99 pre-inference latency reduced by >=20%.
- Tail improvements should not regress throughput by >5% for batched workloads.

Planned experiments (bench categories):
A. Microbench: JSON parsing variants (single-threaded)
  - Purpose: isolate parse cost given identical payload.
  - Payload templates: tiny-command (40-120 bytes), small-chat (400-900 bytes), embeddings-request (2KB).
  - Parsers: Python json, ujson, orjson, simdjson python binding, custom partial parser (header-only using simple split).
  - Metrics: CPU user/sys time, allocations (tracemalloc or heapy), wall time, interpreter time (py-spy).
  - Output: per-parser median/p95/p99 across 10k iterations, mem alloc delta.

B. Microbench: Tokenizer critical path (single-threaded)
  - Purpose: measure unicode scanning and BPE cost across payload shapes and charsets.
  - Tokenizers: current python-based tokenizer, C-accelerated tokenizer (rust/c), pretokenized cache lookup.
  - Variants: ascii-heavy prompt, emoji/UTF8-heavy prompt, long-prefix repeated token.
  - Metrics: tokens/sec, CPU cycles per token, heap churn.

C. Handoff / thread pool scheduling (multi-threaded)
  - Purpose: measure cost of request ingestion -> worker thread -> runtime RPC handoff for both small and medium requests.
  - Setup: lightweight local harness mimicking request pipeline: listener thread(s) -> parse -> validation -> worker-queue push -> worker pop -> run-native-tokenize -> simulate-gpu-infer-sleep.
  - Variables: thread pool type (ThreadPoolExecutor, custom cooperative pool), queue depth, use of park/unpark vs condition variable.
  - Metrics: end-to-end latency distribution, scheduling wakeups per request, context switches (perf stat), lock hold times.

D. Combined synthetic service benchmark (end-to-end)
  - Purpose: show realistic effect on p95/p99 under concurrency and a mixture of payloads.
  - Workloads: 80% tiny/20% mid; 50/50; embeddings-heavy.
  - Deploy variants: baseline (current trunk), fast-json (orjson/simdjson), fast-tokenizer (c-impl), reduced-copy-path (shallow-slices & memoryviews), combination.
  - Metrics: p50/p95/p99 pre-inference CPU, total request CPU, system-wide throughput, GC pauses, lock contention.

Measurement tooling and artifacts:
- Use py-spy (native) + asyncprofile for sampling flamegraphs; also collect linux perf on kernel events for contention.
- Heap snapshots via tracemalloc for allocation sites.
- A deterministic synthetic driver (go-based) to generate HTTP/GRPC traffic with configurable payload mix and exact interarrival times. Repository: linked PR under test harness (see linked_artifacts).
- Use a small set of replayed real payloads from production sampler (sampled ids provided) with PII stripped.

Bench reproducibility notes:
- Pin CPU governor to performance, set RT throttling off for test VMs.
- Use identical container images across variants (only swap the parser/tokenizer artifact), disable debug logging.
- For each scenario run 5 warmup minutes + 30 minute measured window and 3 independent repeats.

Quick experiments to run first (week 1):
- JSON microbench comparing Python json vs orjson vs simdjson on tiny payloads (10k iterations). Owner: Daniel.
- Tokenizer microbench on ascii vs emoji payloads using current tokenizer vs rust-c binding (local build). Owner: Marta.
- Lightweight pipeline handoff harness to measure scheduling cost baseline. Owner: Aisha.

Data to capture for triage (per-run):
- Flamegraph SVGs (py-spy) annotated with sample counts.
- perf stat summary (context-switches, CPU migrations, syscalls).
- tracemalloc top-20 allocation sites.
- CSV of latency distribution and tokens/sec.

Potential low-effort mitigations to validate quickly:
- Switch to orjson/simdjson for request body parsing (if microbench wins).
- Add an early header-only parse path to short-circuit full JSON when payload is simple (e.g., prompt-only).
- Introduce per-worker pretokenization cache keyed on prompt hash for repetitive tiny prompts.
- Replace ThreadPoolExecutor in hot path with a sticky cooperative IO pool that reduces wakeups.

Risk/unknowns:
- simdjson python binding may allocate in ways that still cause Python-level copying; microbench must include allocation accounting.
- Tokenizer C binding integration may introduce build complexity for Private customers; need a fallback path.
- Production variability (network/TLS) can mask CPU latency improvements unless sampling is targeted.

Next steps / action items:
- [ ] Daniel: produce json parsing microbench benchmark script and run on local perf VM (due 2025-11-18).
- [ ] Marta: build and publish rust tokenizer binary and microbench harness (due 2025-11-20).
- [ ] Aisha: implement handoff harness and initial sampling from production traces (due 2025-11-19).
- [ ] Team: schedule 90-minute perf sync to review initial results (proposed 2025-11-21).

Notes + open questions:
- Are there existing storage caches we can reuse for pretokenization? (storage team?)
- Would a switch to memoryviews in our parse path reduce copies enough to be worth the change? We should microbench slice vs copy costs.
- Do we have reproducible payload fingerprints for top 10 customers to test real patterns? If so, request anonymized samples from Customer Success (CS request id: SERV-REQ-924).

Appendix: example microbench pseudo-invocation
- python -m bench.parse_compare --payload-template tiny --parser orjson --iterations 10000 --capture-tracemalloc out/tiny-orjson-heap.json
- go-runner --mix tiny=0.8,medium=0.2 --qps 100 --duration 00:30:00 --target http://localhost:8080/v1/generate --save-trace out/mix-80-20.json

Proposed filename for archival: parse-vs-tokenize-cpu-hypotheses-bench-plan.json

Comments welcome — this is intentionally pragmatic and narrow so we can iterate quickly.
